blocks.title: Interferometer
blocks.text: An interferometer is an optical tool used in detecting gravitational waves. It is a very sensitive detection device that may use the interference of LASER (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) beams. The basic Michelson interferometer is shown in Fig. 8.9.

An interferometer that detects gravitational waves is a highly sensitive instrument that uses laser light to measure tiny changes in distance between mirrors, caused by gravitational waves passing through the detectors. These interferometers are called LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory). The main differences between LIGO and conventional interferometers are: (a) LIGO is 1000 times larger than a conventional device, and (b) LIGO uses a laser whereas a conventional interferometer has a normal light source.
Basic components of a GW interferometer

items: Laser: produces a stable, high-intensity beam of light.
Power recycling mirror: continually reflects laser light that has already travelled through the instrument back into the interferometer, hence the term recycling.
Beam splitter: divides the laser beam into two perpendicular beams.
Mirrors: reflect the beams, creating two perpendicular arms.
Fabry-Perot cavity: consists of two mirrors facing each other; its purpose is to enhance the path length.
Photodetectors: measure the returning beams, detecting tiny phase shifts, if any.
Arm cavities: enhance the laser light, increasing sensitivity.

blocks.text: A laser beam is split into two perpendicular beams, each travelling down one of two identical paths (arms) of the interferometer. The beams bounce off mirrors at the ends of each arm and return to the starting point, where they are recombined. If a gravitational wave passes through, it causes a tiny disturbance in the distance between the mirrors, resulting in a phase shift between the two beams. When the beams recombine they create an interference pattern, which is measured by a photodetector; the tiny phase shift caused by the gravitational wave alters the interference pattern, allowing the detector to sense the wave's presence. Interference fringes are seen in a Michelson interferometer (For Your Information).

Figure 8.9 is the simplest figure of an interferometer; in reality it is much more complex. On 14 September 2015 the universe's gravitational waves were observed for the very first time by LIGO. The gravitational waves, predicted by Albert Einstein 100 years earlier, came from a collision between two black holes; it took 1.3 billion years for the waves to arrive at the LIGO detector in the USA. For their work on the observation of GWs, Rainer Weiss, Barry C. Barish and Kip S. Thorne (printed 'Barisk' and 'Throne') received the Nobel Prize in 2017. One of the team members, Nergis Mavalvala, a professor at MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), belongs to Pakistan.

Similar to LIGO, there is another facility for measuring gravitational waves, called Virgo, which works under the European Gravitational Observatory (EGO) at Cascina near Pisa, Italy. Virgo is also an interferometer, with two arms of 3 km, whereas LIGO has 4 km arms. The Virgo Observatory is named after the Virgo constellation, which is visible in the night sky during March, April and May. The Virgo cluster is a group of about 1500 galaxies about 50 million light years away; one light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 x 10^12 km (printed as '9.5 billion km'). Virgo has been involved in detecting gravitational wave events, with its first detection in 2017.

blocks.title: Example 8.5
blocks.text: If gravitational waves have a wavelength of 4000 km, find their frequency. Solution: lambda = 4000 km = 4 x 10^6 m, c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, f = ?. As v = f lambda and v = c, f = c/lambda = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 / 4 x 10^6 m = 0.75 x 10^2 s^-1 = 75 Hz.

blocks.title: Example 8.6
blocks.text: A binary system emits gravitational waves with a frequency of 10^-1 Hz. What is the wavelength of these waves? Solution: f = 10^-1 Hz = 10^-1 s^-1, c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, lambda = ?. As v = f lambda and v = c, lambda = c/f = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 / 10^-1 s^-1 = 3 x 10^9 m.

blocks.prompt: What is the primary method used to detect gravitational waves, and what is the significance of detecting them (MCQ 8.12; constructed response 8.5)? If gravitational waves have a wavelength of 3000 km, find their frequency (numerical 8.11).
blocks.explanation: Laser interferometry: an interferometer such as LIGO splits a laser beam down two long perpendicular arms and detects the tiny phase shift when a passing wave changes the arm lengths. Detecting gravitational waves confirms a prediction of general relativity, lets us study strong-field gravity and events such as black hole mergers that give out little or no light, and opens a new window on the universe. f = c/lambda = 3 x 10^8 / 3 x 10^6 = 100 Hz.

items: Interferometer: splits a laser beam into two perpendicular arms, reflects and recombines them; a passing gravitational wave changes the arm lengths, shifting the phase and the interference pattern seen by the photodetector. LIGO is 1000 times larger than a conventional interferometer and uses a laser.

Components: laser, power recycling mirror, beam splitter, mirrors, Fabry-Perot cavity, photodetectors, arm cavities. LIGO 14 September 2015 (black holes, Nobel 2017); Virgo 3 km arms, first detection 2017. Examples: 75 Hz; 3 x 10^9 m.
